findings.quote: nearly all of the atom's mass and charge is in a very small nucleus, which is positive because the atom is neutral and its electrons are negative
findings.problem: New in the round-3 fix. The base said 'nearly all of the atom's positive charge and mass'; the fix dropped 'positive', so the sentence now says nearly all of the atom's charge is in the nucleus. That is false: the electrons carry negative charge equal in size to the nucleus's positive charge, and the same bullet says so. Rutherford's conclusion is that all of the positive charge and nearly all of the mass are in the nucleus. The round-3 sign issue itself is fixed in the sentence before ('a concentrated charge').
findings.source: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, section 2.2 (Rutherford: the positive charge and nearly all the mass are concentrated in a very small nucleus); checklist B01; reader-rules boundary test

findings.quote: The nucleus holds **protons**, which have positive charge, and **neutrons**, which have no charge.
findings.problem: Stated for every atom (the sentence before says 'Every atom has a center called the **nucleus**'), this fails a known exception: the most common hydrogen atom, hydrogen-1 (protium), has one proton and no neutrons. The lesson then teaches isotopes, where hydrogen's isotopes (0, 1 and 2 neutrons) are a standard case, so a student can come away believing every atom has neutrons.
findings.source: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, section 2.3, hydrogen isotopes protium (0 neutrons), deuterium and tritium; reader-rules 'Added after the Sol audit' boundary test; checklist B01

findings.quote: Which of these is an observation and which is an inference?
findings.problem: The stem gives only one sentence, and both its parts are observations ('Most alpha particles pass through gold foil, but a few bounce at large angles'). There is no inference among 'these' to classify. The solution supplies its own inference ('the atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus') that the question never states. The example teaches the observation-versus-inference skill that the brief's scattering item names, so a stem the student cannot answer as worded harms that skill.
findings.source: Checklist L05; LSG Examples section (supply necessary problem-specific givens); brief item 'Evidence-to-conclusion reasoning from scattering'

findings.problem: Round-3 finding still open. The cathode-ray paragraph that starts here has six sentences. The isotope paragraph that starts 'This contradicts Dalton's claim that all atoms of one element have the same mass.' has five, as do the Bohr photon paragraph starting 'In Bohr's model, an electron in a level does not give off light.' and the quantum-mechanics paragraph. Paragraphs should be one to three short sentences.
findings.source: LSG: Formatting rules; checklist L22a; round-3 read L22a
